items.text: O learned one, kindly attend to our proposition.
We maintain that this empirical world, whose ultimate status is under dispute, is mithyaa.
Our reason is drishyatva: its being an object of cognition.
Consider the silver that appears upon a piece of mother of pearl.
Although silver is perceived, upon closer examination, we discover that no silver exists there.
Similarly, we propose that whatever is an object of cognition is mithyaa, like the silver appearing in mother of pearl.
This world, too, is an object of cognition.
Therefore, we conclude that the world is mithyaa.
Just as the appearance of silver is negated by correct knowledge of the shell, the claim that the world possesses ultimate, independent reality must also be subjected to examination.
One moment, venerable scholar!
Before accepting your conclusion, we must first examine the precise nature of what you seek to establish.
What exactly do you mean by mithyaatva?
If you mean absolute non-existence, how do you account for the silver that is actually experienced upon the mother of pearl?
But if you define it as sadasad-vilakshanatva, that which is distinct from both ultimate existence and absolute non-existence, then another difficulty arises.
What precisely constitutes existence?
And what constitutes non-existence?
How can the absence of existence, and the absence of non-existence, seemingly opposed to one another, reside in the same locus?
Until the definition itself is established without contradiction, how can the conclusion resting upon it be accepted?
An excellent question, learned one!
We do not maintain that the world is utterly non-existent, like the horn of a hare.
By existence, we mean trikaala-abaadhyatva: that which remains unsublated throughout the three periods of time.
Past, present, and future.
By absolute non-existence, we mean that which is incapable of ever appearing as existent, in any locus.
Consider again the silver perceived upon mother of pearl.
It appears to consciousness.
Yet, when correct knowledge arises, that appearance is sublated.
Thus, it is neither ultimately real, like Brahman, nor utterly incapable of appearance, like a hare’s horn.
This is what we mean by sadasad-vilakshanatva.
And now, let us turn to the testimony of the Chhaandogya Upanishad.
Sad eva somya, idam agra aaseet, ekam eva adviteeyam.
In the beginning, dear one, this was Being alone, one without a second.
And elsewhere, the same scripture declares.
Vaachaarambhanam vikaaro naamadheyam, mrittiketyeva satyam.
A modification is merely a name arising through speech; clay alone is real.
Reflect upon this carefully, venerable scholar.
A pot possesses a distinct name and form.
Yet, without clay, where is the pot?
Its apparent individuality depends entirely upon its underlying material reality.
Likewise, we maintain that this universe of names and forms possesses no independent ultimate existence apart from Brahman.
And it is precisely here, respected scholar, that our inquiry must deepen!
We readily acknowledge that the pot depends upon clay.
But from where does it follow, that dependence necessarily implies mithyaatva?
A pot can hold water.
An unshaped lump of clay cannot perform that function in the same manner.
The distinctive properties of the pot are established through direct perception.
Therefore, the dependence of an object upon its cause, does not, by itself, establish that the object is unreal.
Consider also your example of the silver appearing upon mother of pearl.
In that case, a correcting cognition arises: This is not silver.
Thus, the mistaken appearance is demonstrably sublated.
But in the case of this waking world, what corresponding valid means of knowledge establishes its sublation?
Furthermore, consider the declaration of the Katha Upanishad.
Eko bahoonaam, yo vidadhaati kaamaan.
The One who fulfills the desires of the many.
Here, the relationship between the One and the many is expressed.
The intended meaning of this distinction must also be examined.
Dependence upon another does not, by itself, establish the non-reality of that which depends.
Your question is reasonable.
We do not deny that a pot possesses the capacity to hold water.
Indeed, we fully acknowledge vyaavahaarika sattaa: reality at the level of ordinary experience and practical activity.
Yet, the successful functioning of an object within experience does not, by itself, establish its paaramaarthika sattaa: ultimate reality.
Consider the experience of a dream.
Within the dream, pleasure, suffering, movement, and countless other experiences appear meaningful.
Yet, upon awakening, the dream world is sublated.
Through this example, we demonstrate only that practical experience does not automatically establish ultimate reality.
We do not claim that the waking world and the dream world are identical in every respect.
According to our position, the ultimate sublation of the empirical world is accomplished through knowledge of Brahman.
Then let us return to the very foundation of your inference.
You have declared: Because it possesses drishyatva.
But what precisely is the definition of drishyatva?
Do you mean vritti-vyaapyatva: being encompassed by a cognition’s mental modification?
Or phala-vyaapyatva: being encompassed by the resulting manifestation of knowledge?
Or perhaps asva-prakaashatva: not being self-luminous?
In the example of the silver appearing upon mother of pearl, its sublation is established.
But by what valid means of knowledge have you established an invariable relationship between drishyatva and mithyaatva, throughout the entire empirical world?
One example alone does not establish vyaapti: an invariable relation between the reason, and what is to be proved.
Therefore, the fundamental question remains.
How can drishyatva be established as an avyabhichaari linga, an unfailing logical indicator, of mithyaatva?
Thus concludes the first dialogue.
The definition of mithyaatva has been examined.
The examples have been presented, and questioned.
Yet the question of vyaapti remains unresolved.
In our next dialogue, we shall examine whether drishyatva truly constitutes a valid reason for establishing mithyaatva.
Until then, let the inquiry into truth continue.
